library(cytokineR)
library(data.table)

This vignette explains the ideas behind the signal representations and
calibration methods in cytokineR, and why the conventional route -- one
five-parameter logistic standard curve per plate -- is not always the best
choice.

## A simple model of what goes wrong between plates

For an analyte with true concentration $C$ in the well, the median
fluorescence intensity on plate $p$ is approximately

$$
\mathrm{FI} = 2^{\gamma_p}\Big[B\,2^{\beta_p} + (T - B)\,
S\big(\log_2 C + \eta_p\big)\Big],
$$

where $S$ is a sigmoid, $B$ and $T$ are the background and the saturation
level, and three plate effects act on top:

| effect | symbol | physical cause (examples) | shape on the log2 FI scale |
|---|---|---|---|
| gain | $\gamma_p$ | reader calibration, detection antibody / SAPE amount | vertical shift of the whole curve |
| potency | $\eta_p$ | incubation time and temperature, antibody lot | horizontal shift of the curve |
| background | $\beta_p$ | matrix, washing, blocking | moves only the lower asymptote |

Between kit lots (batches) the same effects occur, and in addition the
*assigned* concentrations of the standards are themselves uncertain: every
lot's standard has its own true concentration, and an error there shifts every
concentration calibrated from it.

The simulator (`simulate_cyto()`) generates data from exactly this model, which
is what lets us check methods against the truth.

## Signal representations

`cyto_transform()` defines what is being measured. All representations are on
a log2 scale, so a difference of 1 is a two-fold change.

| method | value | removes | cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| `log2` | $\log_2$ FI | nothing | -- |
| `bgsub` | $\log_2$(FI $-$ blank) | additive background | noisy near zero |
| `mob` | $\log_2$(FI / blank) | gain (if blanks track it) | as noisy as the blanks |
| `mos` | $\log_2$(FI / FI$_{\text{ref. standard}}$) | gain, local potency | depends on one standard |
| `moc` | $\log_2$(FI / FI$_{\text{control}}$) | gain, local potency | needs the same control on every plate |

The ratio representations need no curve fitting and are never censored. They
give relative, not absolute, units -- which is all most analyses (group
comparisons, correlations, changes over time) need. Breen et al. (2016,
*Sci Rep* 6:26996) showed that raw fluorescence often has better statistical
properties than the derived concentrations, particularly for low-abundance
analytes.

### Multiple of blank

Dividing by the plate's blank removes the plate gain only to the extent that
the blank wells move with it. Blanks are also the noisiest wells (low FI,
often only one or two per plate), so `mob` shrinks each plate's blank level
towards the batch mean by empirical Bayes (`shrink = TRUE`): plates with
consistent blank replicates keep their own value, plates with erratic blanks
borrow from the others.

```{r}
m <- cyto_transform(cyto_example, "mob")
head(cyto_fit(m))
```

Independently of normalisation, multiple-of-blank is a natural *detectability*
scale: the fraction of samples with FI more than twice the blank is a quick,
curve-free summary of which analytes are measurable at all.

```{r}
m$data[sample_type == "unknown", .(above_2x_blank = mean(value > 1)),
       by = analyte][order(above_2x_blank)]
```

### Multiple of standard

`mos` divides by the FI of one standard on the same plate. With
`level = "auto"` the reference is, per analyte, the standard whose FI is
closest to the typical sample, so the correction is most accurate where the
samples are. Because standards of different kit lots have different assigned
concentrations, `by_conc = TRUE` instead interpolates each plate's FI at a
fixed *concentration* (log-log between the neighbouring standards), which
makes the ratio comparable across lots.

```{r}
s <- cyto_transform(cyto_example, "mos", by_conc = TRUE)
head(cyto_fit(s))
```

### Multiple of control

`moc` anchors every plate to the control material(s) measured on it -- the
same idea as inter-plate controls in Olink's NPX scale. Any material works if
it is (i) the same physical material on every plate and (ii) in the
measurable range: a pooled serum or plasma is ideal. With several materials
the plate level is estimated robustly from all of them.

## Plate and batch correction

`cyto_normalize()` estimates a correction per plate (or batch) and analyte and
applies it to *all* wells of that plate. The methods differ in what they
assume:

* **Comparable samples** (`median`, `quantile`): every plate holds a similar
  mix of samples. True for randomised layouts; with `within = "time"` (or
  study, group, ...) the comparison is made within strata, which protects
  layouts where plates differ in composition.
* **Anchor material** (`anchor`, `bridge`): some material is measured on
  several plates or batches -- controls, standards, bridging samples. No
  assumption about the study samples is needed, but the anchor must behave
  like the samples. With `fit = "affine"` and anchors that span the range
  (standards), compression of the signal is corrected too.
* **Known covariates** (`regress`): plate effects are removed from a linear
  model that also contains the biological covariates, so unbalanced designs
  are handled if the covariates are known.

## Why per-plate standard curves are fragile

A 5PL curve has five parameters, typically estimated from eight levels in
duplicate. Several things then go wrong:

1. **The low end sits near the asymptote.** Where many cytokines are measured,
   the curve is flat, so small FI noise becomes large concentration noise and
   the lower limit of quantification differs from plate to plate.
2. **One bad standard well bends the whole curve.** With few points per
   curve, a pipetting error moves every concentration on that plate.
3. **Censoring becomes plate-dependent.** Because the working range differs
   between plates, the same sample can be "OOR <" on one plate and quantified
   on another; missingness then carries a plate effect.
4. **Lot errors pass straight through.** Every concentration inherits the
   error of the lot's assigned standard concentrations; only material
   measured in several batches can remove it.

A small experiment makes points 1--3 concrete. On one plate, we double the
FI of a single standard well -- in turn at every level and for three
analytes -- and record how far the calibrated values of the samples and
controls on that plate move, and how many previously quantified values are
lost to censoring:

```{r}
methods <- list("5PL per plate" = list("5pl"),
                "spline per plate" = list("spline"),
                "shared 5PL (robust)" = list("shared"))
res <- list()
for (an in c("IL-8", "IP-10", "VEGF")) {
  base <- cyto_filter(cyto_example, analyte == an)
  ref <- lapply(methods, function(m) do.call(cyto_calibrate, c(list(base), m))$data)
  for (lv in 1:8) {
    x <- base
    x$data <- data.table::copy(x$data)      # data.table: copy before editing
    w <- x$data[plate == "b1p2" & sample_type == "standard" & level == lv, .row][1]
    x$data[.row == w, fi := fi * 2]
    x <- cyto_transform(x, "log2")          # recompute value from fi
    for (mn in names(methods)) {
      new <- do.call(cyto_calibrate, c(list(x), methods[[mn]]))$data
      old <- ref[[mn]]
      i <- old$sample_type != "standard" & old$plate == "b1p2"
      both <- i & is.finite(old$value) & is.finite(new$value)
      res[[length(res) + 1]] <- data.table(
        method = mn,
        shift = if (any(both)) stats::median(abs(new$value[both] - old$value[both]))
                else NA_real_,
        lost = mean(is.finite(old$value[i]) & !is.finite(new$value[i])))
    }
  }
}
rbindlist(res)[, .(mean_abs_shift_log2 = round(mean(shift, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
                   worst_shift_log2 = round(max(shift, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
                   values_lost = round(mean(lost), 3),
                   plate_lost_entirely = sum(is.na(shift))), by = method]
```

The per-plate 5PL both moves the results and loses values: the bad point
distorts the whole curve and shrinks the working range, sometimes to nothing
(the whole plate is lost for that analyte). The monotone interpolation keeps
its range, but samples in the affected segment can move a lot. The
shared-shape curve is the most stable: within a kit lot all plates share the curve *shape*, each plate only
gets shrunken shifts for gain, potency and background
(`shift = c("x", "y", "bottom")`), and the fit uses a robust (Huber) loss, so
a single bad well is outvoted. A plate whose standards all failed can even
borrow the shared curve (flagged `borrowed_curve`). For per-plate fits,
`robust = TRUE` and `drop_outliers = 1` are available too.

## Normalising before calibrating -- and why it is often undone

A plate correction applied to all wells moves the standards together with
the samples. A per-plate calibration then re-maps that plate's standards to
their assigned concentrations, which cancels the correction:

```{r}
direct <- cyto_calibrate(cyto_example, "5pl")
normalised_first <- cyto_example |>
  cyto_transform("log2") |>
  cyto_normalize("median") |>
  cyto_calibrate("5pl")
all.equal(direct$data$value, normalised_first$data$value, tolerance = 1e-4)
```

To keep a correction, fit fewer curves: **harmonise first, calibrate once.**
Align the plates of each lot on their standards (affine anchor), align the
lots on bridging samples, then fit one curve per analyte on the reference
lot's standards:

```{r}
h <- cyto_example |>
  cyto_transform("log2") |>
  cyto_normalize("anchor", anchors = "standard", scope = "batch",
                 fit = "affine") |>
  cyto_correct_batch("bridge") |>
  cyto_calibrate("5pl", curve_by = NULL, standards = ~ batch == "1")
cyto_fit(h, "calibrate")$curves[, c("analyte", "lloq", "uloq")]
```

Now all plates and both lots share one working range, so censoring is no
longer plate-dependent, and the result is on the reference lot's
concentration scale.

## Censored values

Signal representations are never censored. Concentrations are, and the
choice of imputation matters:

* `fraction` (e.g. LLOQ/2) is simple but piles values on one number and
  shrinks the variance.
* `tobit` fits a censored normal distribution per analyte (optionally with
  covariates) and replaces each censored value by its conditional
  expectation below its limit.
* `rank_tobit` does the same but keeps the information that is still in the
  fluorescence signal: within a plate, censored values are ordered by their
  FI and spread over the quantiles of the truncated distribution. A sample
  with FI twice the blank stays above one at the blank.

```{r}
cx <- cyto_calibrate(cyto_example, "5pl")
cx <- cyto_impute(cx, "rank_tobit")
cx$data[censored == "left" & plate == "b1p1" & analyte == "IL-10",
        .(sample_id, fi = round(fi), value = round(value, 2))][order(fi)][1:8]
```

## Which is best?

That depends on the assay, the layout and what is on every plate -- which is
why cytokineR treats it as an empirical question. `vignette("benchmarking")`
shows how to compare strategies on your own data without fooling yourself.
